steps.title: Mix sauce
points: Combine the soy sauce, sugar, sake, and water in a small bowl.
Add the ginger now if you are using it.
steps.hint: If you start measuring after the heat is on, the pork overcooks while you do it. Making the sauce first is the single most effective move in this recipe.

steps.title: Slice onion
points: Peel the onion and halve it lengthwise.
Slice with the grain into pieces about 5 mm thick.
Wash the board and knife now: the pork needs no cutting.

steps.title: Brown pork
points: Heat the oil over medium-high, or skip the oil if the pork is fatty.
Spread the pork so the pieces overlap as little as possible, then leave it alone for 1 to 2 minutes.
Flip only once the underside is well browned.
steps.hint: Stirring too early draws out moisture and you end up steaming the meat instead of searing it.

steps.title: Soften onion
points: Push the meat to one side and add the onion to the empty half.
Cook for about 2 minutes, until translucent with lightly colored edges.

steps.title: Reduce sauce
points: Pour in the sauce and keep it at a lively bubble, shaking the pan, for 1 to 2 minutes.
Kill the heat once it thickens, clings to the meat, and turns glossy.
Add the butter off the heat and let the residual warmth melt it.
steps.hint: Over-reduce and it suddenly turns salty. Stop while a little sauce still pools at the bottom of the pan.

steps.title: Heat rice
points: Heat the packed rice as directed.
Tip it into a deep bowl.

steps.title: Assemble bowl
points: Pile the pork and onion over the rice.
Scrape every last bit of sauce from the pan over the top.

troubleshooting.problem: The pork is tough or dry
troubleshooting.solution: It was overcooked. Thin-sliced pork is nearly done the moment it's browned. About 30 seconds after flipping is plenty, and the sauce finishes the rest.

troubleshooting.problem: The meat weeps water and won't brown
troubleshooting.solution: The pan wasn't hot enough, or the meat was piled up. Wait until the oil shimmers with a wisp of smoke, then spread the pieces flat. 150 g is the most one pan can sear at once.
The sauce wasn't reduced enough. Stopped while still watery, it soaks into the rice and turns thin. Boil it down until it's glossy and slightly thick.
Reduced too far. Add 1 tablespoon of water and bring it back to a brief simmer. Next time use 3 tablespoons of water for more margin.
It needed more heat. Cook until translucent, then give it one more minute in the sauce and the sharpness turns to sweetness.
Chopped scallions, shichimi pepper, an egg yolk, or mayonnaise. Pick exactly one. Stacking several muddies the flavor.
